tldr: Researchers developed "Reflex," a system that enables a humanoid robot to catch a flying box using its whole body in about one second. By dividing the problem into three stages—whole-body control, object dynamics prediction, and visual grounding—it catches boxes on a real Unitree G1 using only onboard RGB-D camera feeds, achieving about 60% to 70% of human catch success rates.
hero_caption: An overview of the Reflex training pipeline. Stage 1 trains whole-body motion via reinforcement learning. Stage 2 compresses box dynamics—including delays and dropouts—into a latent representation. Stage 3 directly estimates this latent representation from onboard RGB-D video while keeping the controller frozen.
overview:
Humans effortlessly catch flying balls or parcels with their whole body. Achieving this on a bipedal humanoid, however, has been exceptionally difficult. For an object arriving in just about one second, the robot must coordinate whole-body control to step, pose, absorb impact, and maintain balance. It must also predict trajectories under sensor delays and visually track the object from an onboard camera while moving vigorously. Prior robotic systems relied on external cameras or marked objects, or were limited to fixed-base arms.

Instead of learning whole-body motion and visual perception end-to-end, the authors introduced Reflex, a framework that decouples training into three stages via a compact 8-dimensional latent representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body control using privileged simulator state (Stage 1). Next, it extracts the latent representation from box states that include observation delays (Stage 2). Finally, the controller is frozen, and an egocentric RGB-D camera history is trained to regress this latent representation (Stage 3). Separating image rendering to only the final visual learning stage also dramatically improves sample efficiency.

In simulation, Reflex achieved an 85.7% catch success rate using only onboard RGB-D images, closely matching the 87.9% achieved with direct privileged state. On a real Unitree G1 humanoid, it successfully caught human-thrown boxes with a 65% success rate at 2.5 m and 40% at 5 m, reaching about 76% and 59% of human catchers' success rates (85.0% and 68.3%) at the same distances.
contributions: Realized whole-body coordinated catching of flying boxes on a humanoid using only onboard RGB-D vision, without relying on external markers or motion capture.

Proposed an efficient three-stage learning framework that decomposes whole-body control, delay-tolerant object dynamics representation, and visual grounding, decoupling expensive image rendering from reinforcement learning.
Demonstrated on a real Unitree G1 that the robot can reliably catch and hold cardboard boxes thrown by humans from 2.5 m (65% success) and 5 m (40% success) using its whole body.

sections.heading: Catching a Flying Box: Three Hurdles Humanoids Face
sections.summary: Instinctively catching a flying object with the whole body like a human is largely uncharted territory for humanoids. It requires solving three tightly coupled challenges: whole-body balance, trajectory prediction under sensor latency, and egocentric visual perception during aggressive self-motion. The authors propose Reflex, a three-stage framework, to tackle real-world box catching.
sections.details:
Humans effortlessly catch a falling cup or receive a tossed parcel. For a robot, however, this task is exceptionally difficult. It must anticipate the landing spot and absorb the impact with its whole body while maintaining balance, all within about a single second.

Three challenges arise simultaneously:
- **Whole-body coordinated control**: Unlike simply swatting an object away with an end-effector, the robot must reposition its feet and torso, form a cradle with its forearms and chest to absorb impact, and prevent falls.
- **Fast reaction under latency**: On real hardware, there is only about one second from toss to arrival. Yet the camera detection pipeline alone introduces a median delay of around 69 ms. Simply reacting to the latest frame is too late; the robot must anticipate and initiate motion early.
- **Perception from an egocentric viewpoint**: Because the robot moves vigorously, egomotion is mixed into the object's movement in camera frames. Furthermore, the robot's own arms occlude the box right before contact.

Most prior works relied on external motion capture, stationary cameras, or marked objects. Reflex accomplishes the task entirely with onboard RGB-D vision. By decomposing learning into privileged reinforcement learning (Stage 1), acquiring a latent representation robust to delays and dropouts (Stage 2), and predicting the latent representation from visual inputs (Stage 3), it completely isolates heavy image rendering from the RL loop. Experiments on a real Unitree G1 show it catches human throws with a 65% success rate from 2.5 m and 40% from 5 m.

sections.heading: At the Crossroads of Catching, Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation, and Privileged Learning
sections.summary: The authors review prior work in flying object catching, humanoid whole-body control, and privileged sim-to-real transfer. Most existing systems rely on fixed bases or external tracking. Bipedal humanoid whole-body catching using only onboard vision has remained largely unexplored.
sections.details:
This research builds upon three main research areas:

### Catching Flying Objects
Catching flying objects with robotic arms has a long history. Recently, researchers have demonstrated catching with mobile-base arms, quadrupeds, wheeled humanoids, as well as bipedal humanoids punching balls or catching basketballs. However, most rely on external motion capture or external cameras to track object positions. Very few have attempted autonomous whole-body catching using solely onboard cameras.

### Whole-Body Control and Mobile Manipulation
Imitation learning from human motion capture data (such as Adversarial Motion Priors, or AMP) has become the de facto standard for humanoid control. Recent works have enabled humanoids to pick up and carry heavy boxes. However, those tasks involve stationary boxes on the floor lifted at the robot's own pace. Catching a flying object fundamentally differs because the robot cannot choose the contact timing; it must be fully pre-positioned before impact.

### Privileged Learning and Visual Sim-to-Real Transfer
Privileged learning—where a teacher policy trains with full simulator state and a student model mimics its representations using real sensors—has shown great success in quadruped rough-terrain locomotion (e.g., RMA) and humanoid obstacle traversal. However, prior setups focused on static terrain or slowly moving objects. This work extends privileged learning to aggressive visual self-motion and fast-moving dynamic objects.

sections.heading: Embracing Human Throws: Task Design and Evaluation Metrics
sections.summary: The authors formulate the task of catching and holding human-thrown cardboard boxes against the chest using a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid. They establish strict criteria to distinguish merely stopping the box (interception) from securely holding it for at least 0.6 seconds (catch success).
sections.details:
### Dynamic Catching Task via Onboard Vision
The hardware platform is the 29-degree-of-freedom (DoF) Unitree G1 humanoid. Its only inputs are a 192×144 RGB-D stream from a chest-mounted camera and proprioceptive robot states such as joint states and IMU readings. No external cameras or object tracking sensors are used. Control runs at 50 Hz (20 ms period), and the policy outputs 29-DoF target joint positions. Isaac Lab serves as the physics simulator, running physics at 200 Hz and control at 50 Hz.

### Success Criteria
To objectively separate mere contact from secure catches, the authors define the following criteria:
- **Interception**: Reducing the flying box's velocity to below 1 m/s near the torso, fully arresting its momentum. Dropping it afterward still counts as an interception.
- **Catch Success**: The primary evaluation metric. The box is supported against the chest area, both wrists flank the box on either side, it does not rest on the head or shoulders, and it is held at low velocity for at least 0.6 seconds.
- **Postural Stability (Torso Excursion / Falls)**: Catching the box is meaningless if the robot loses balance and falls. Torso pitch exceeding 38° from throw to finish (Torso Excursion) and falls are tracked separately.

sections.heading: A Three-Stage Framework: Whole-Body Motion, Latency Tolerance, and Vision
sections.summary: Learning directly from images via RL is computationally prohibitive and difficult to explore, so learning is split into three stages. Stage 1 trains whole-body motor skills via PPO. Stage 2 extracts an 8-dimensional dynamics latent from delayed box states. Stage 3 regresses this latent directly from camera streams.
sections.details:
The core of Reflex is decoupling the visual encoder $V_{\psi}$ from the whole-body controller $\pi_{\theta}$. The policy estimates an 8-dimensional latent vector $\mathbf{z}$ from the RGB-D history and converts it, along with proprioceptive state, into 29-DoF target joint positions. Training proceeds through three stages:

### Stage 1: Learning Whole-Body Control Skills
In a fast simulation environment without image rendering, a state-based teacher policy is trained using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization). Along with approach rewards, chest holding rewards, and success bonuses, human reference motions and AMP (Adversarial Motion Priors) encourage natural, coordinated whole-body movements. It uses full box position and velocity, but injects noise and delays modeled after real Kalman filters to enhance robustness.

### Stage 2: Acquiring Latent Representations of Object Dynamics
A privileged encoder $E_{\phi}$ is trained to map box observations $\mathbf{p}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{26}$ (camera-frame position, relative velocity, size, orientation, etc.) to an 8-dimensional latent vector $\mathbf{z}$. Random delays of 1 to 3 steps (20 to 60 ms) and out-of-view dropouts are applied to observations. It is initialized via behavior matching (behavior cloning) against Stage 1 teacher actions, collects rollouts via DAgger, and is fine-tuned alongside the decoder using PPO. This condenses the motion dynamics needed by the controller into 8 dimensions, even from delayed and incomplete information.

### Stage 3: Grounding the Latent Representation in Egocentric Vision
The Stage 2 privileged encoder and control decoder are completely frozen. A visual encoder is trained via supervised learning to predict latent vector $\mathbf{z}$ directly from a 25-frame history of onboard RGB-D images and camera egomotion history.
- **Network Architecture**: A CNN predicts box position heatmaps. Geometric features from these heatmaps (image coordinates, local depth, back-projected 3D points, etc.) and egomotion are fed into a GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) to regress $\mathbf{z}$.
- **Two-Stage Visual Training with DAgger**: The CNN heatmap detector is pre-trained first, followed by GRU training targeting the latent values. Re-collecting visual data visited by the visual controller using DAgger ensures robustness to viewpoint shake.

### Downstream Task Connection (Carrying and Handover)
After a successful catch, a supervisor confirms the box is held stably and seamlessly hands control over to an existing locomotion controller (SONIC). The robot can then walk over to find a human and hand the box over.

captions.F2: Detailed three-stage training architecture. It illustrates the staged approach: state-based PPO in Stage 1, behavior matching and PPO fine-tuning in Stage 2, and latent regression using RGB-D history and egomotion in Stage 3.

sections.heading: Rigorous Evaluation: Simulation Robustness and Real Unitree G1 Verification
sections.summary: The authors evaluated Reflex both in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. In simulation, Reflex achieved an 85.7% catch rate using only onboard vision. On real hardware, it caught 65% of throws from 2.5 m and 40% from 5 m. Ablations highlight that temporal history, egomotion input, and delay randomization are indispensable.
sections.details:
### Overall Performance (Q1)
In simulation, the proposed visual controller caught 3,290 out of 3,840 throws (85.7%). This matches the 87.9% achieved by the privileged latent controller. On the real Unitree G1, it achieved success rates of 65% at 2.5 m, 40% at 5 m, and 15% at 7 m. Compared to human catching performance under the same conditions (85.0% at 2.5 m, 68.3% at 5 m, 28.3% at 7 m), Reflex reaches 76% of human performance at 2.5 m and 59% at 5 m.

### Whole-Body Control and Reward Contributions (Q2)
In Stage 2 PPO fine-tuning, removing task rewards (approach and holding) caused catch success to collapse to 2.7%. Removing locomotion priors (both tracking and AMP) led to training failure from leg termination errors. The controller maintained 77.7% to 91.2% success rates under unseen payloads (0.5 to 2 kg). On the other hand, for box sizes substantially different from training (extra small or extra large), the robot still achieved interceptions, but holding (catch) success dropped significantly.

### Dynamics and Latency Robustness (Q3)
Behavior matching initialization yielded an average 5.2-point improvement in catch success over naive weight copying. Delay randomization (20 to 60 ms) introduced in Stage 2 proved crucial, maintaining a 5 to 11-point advantage across all latency settings compared to a model trained without delay. The visual controller also proved resilient to laterally offset throws (0.6 m offset), retaining a 66.6% success rate.

### Ablation of Visual Grounding Components (Q4)
Ablation experiments highlighted several essential design choices:
- **Removing Temporal History**: Using only a single frame caused catch success to plummet by 35.6 to 39.8 points. Temporal history is vital for inferring velocity and motion.
- **Removing Egomotion**: Removing camera egomotion reduced success by 10.4 points on centered throws and 22.6 points on 0.6 m offset throws.
- **Latent Regression vs. Full State Regression**: Regressing the full 26-dimensional box state instead of the latent representation dropped success by about 19 points. Avoiding the prediction of task-irrelevant geometry pays off.
- **Comparison to Detector + Kalman Filter**: The proposed latent pipeline outperformed a baseline combining the same CNN detector with an optimally tuned Kalman filter.

captions.F5: Real-world catching experiments on the Unitree G1. Using only onboard cameras, the robot adapts and catches across different throw distances (2.5 m, 5 m, 7 m), box sizes, weights (0.5 kg, 1 kg, 2 kg), and lateral throw offsets (0.9 m right, 0.7 m left).

sections.heading: Key Takeaways and Current Limitations
sections.summary: Decoupling control from vision enabled highly efficient training, requiring only 1.6 million image rendering steps. However, limitations remain, including reduced visual prediction accuracy on long-distance throws and limited adaptability to box size variations.
sections.details:
### Advantages of This Approach
Decoupling whole-body control and visual perception via a compact dynamics latent yields huge benefits. Training end-to-end visual reinforcement learning across all stages would have required massive compute. Here, image rendering was confined to roughly 1.6 million steps, allowing training to complete in a reasonable time on a single RTX 3090 GPU.

### Acknowledged Limitations
The authors note several limitations:
- **Drop-off on Long-Distance Throws**: At 5 m and 7 m distances, box flight speeds reach around 12 m/s, exceeding training assumptions (up to 8.5 m/s). Visual trajectory prediction becomes difficult, lowering success rates (40% at 5 m, 15% at 7 m on real hardware). While adding long-range data to Stage 3 helped in simulation, real-world validation remains future work.
- **Size-blind Policy**: The controller is designed around standard-sized boxes and does not explicitly use box size. Consequently, it often fails to secure extra small or extra large boxes, despite touching them.
- **Real-World Visual Artifacts**: Simulation does not model motion blur, auto-exposure shifts, or structured depth sensor noise.

sections.heading: Looking Ahead: Toward Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control
sections.summary: Reflex achieves dynamic real-world catching on a humanoid by uniting whole-body control, object dynamics estimation, and egocentric vision across three stages. This framework can extend beyond catching to dodging, handovers, and physical assistance, unlocking humanoids capable of reflexive whole-body reactions to sudden environmental changes.
sections.details:
This paper presented Reflex, a control framework for whole-body dynamic box catching using only onboard RGB-D camera feeds.

By separating whole-body control and visual perception through a dynamics latent across three stages, Reflex achieved an 85.7% catch rate in simulation—nearly matching privileged state inputs—and reached roughly 60% to 70% of human catching performance on a real Unitree G1. Demonstrating success on an extreme dynamic task like whole-body catching, the authors conclude that this approach lays important groundwork for humanoids that can react agilely in the real world—such as catching tossed tools, dodging falling objects, or offering rapid physical assistance.

takeaways: Decoupling motor control training with privileged state from visual latent regression avoids end-to-end visual RL, drastically cutting rendering overhead while delivering high-performing policies.
For egocentric humanoid vision under aggressive body motion, feeding temporal history and camera egomotion is critically important compared to relying on single-frame detections.
Randomizing observation delays during simulation training substantially boosts policy robustness against hardware-specific pipeline latencies.
limitations: On high-speed, long-distance throws (5 m or more) that exceed training assumptions, visual prediction struggles and catch success rates drop significantly.
The controller does not explicitly perceive box dimensions to adjust its arm cradle width, often failing to hold extra small or extra large boxes.
Strong motion blur and sudden auto-exposure changes in real-world camera feeds are not simulated, highlighting the need for more robust visual perception.
